breaths.text: Maiden, and mistress of the months and stars
Goddess whom all gods love with threefold heart, Being treble in thy divided deity,
Swift on the hills as morning, and a hand To all things fierce and fleet that roar and range
Hear now and help and lift no violent hand, But favourable and fair as thine eye's beam
Amid the king's hounds and the hunting men Have wrought and worshipped toward thee; nor shall man
But for the end, that lies unreached at yet Between the hands and on the knees of gods,
And dreams and desolation of the night! Rise up, shine, stretch thine hand out, with thy bow Touch the most dimmest height of trembling heaven,
Shot through and through with arrows; let thine hair Lighten as flame above that nameless shell
And thy lips kindle with swift beams; let earth Laugh, and the long sea fiery from thy feet Through all the roar and ripple of streaming springs
Shaken from hands and blown from lips of nymphs Whose hair or breast divides the wandering wave
All gold, or shuddering and unfurrowed snow; And all the winds about thee with their wings,
Each horn of Acheloues, and the green Euenus, wedded with the straitening sea.
Twin-born with him, and virgin, Artemis, And give our spears their spoil, the wild boar's hide.
And bloodless altars without wine or fire. Him now consume thou; for thy sacrifice
And one, the maiden rose of all thy maids, Arcadian Atalanta, snowy-souled,
From Ladon and well-wooded Maenalus Over the firm hills and the fleeting sea
Heroes, the crown of men, like gods in fight. Moreover out of all the Aetolian land,
To what of fruitful field the son of Zeus Won from the roaring river and labouring sea
And foamed and lessened through his wrathful fords, Leaving clear lands that steamed with sudden sun,
Bring thee fresh wreaths and their own sweeter hair, Luxurious locks and flower-like mixed with flowers,
Divides from these things; whom do thou not less Help and give honour, and to mine hounds good speed,
When the hounds of spring are on winter's traces,
Fills the shadows and windy places With lisp of leaves and ripple of rain;
Is half assuaged for Itylus, For the Thracian ships and the foreign faces,
Come with bows bent and with emptying of quivers.
With a noise of winds and many rivers, With a clamour of waters, and with might;
Over the splendour and speed of thy feet; For the faint east quickens, the wan west shivers, Round the feet of the day and the feet of the night.
Where shall we find her, how shall we sing to her,
O that man's heart were as fire and could spring to her, Fire, or the strength of the streams that spring!
As raiment, as songs of the harp-player; For the risen stars and the fallen cling to her,
For winter's rains and ruins are over,
The days dividing lover and lover, The light that loses, the night that wins;
And frosts are slain and flowers begotten, And in green underwood and cover
The full streams feed on flower of rushes,
The faint fresh flame of the young year flushes From leaf to flower and flower to fruit,
And the oat is heard above the lyre, And the hoofed heel of a satyr crushes
And Pan by noon and Bacchus by night,
Follows with dancing and fills with delight The Maenad and the Bassarid;
The laughing leaves of the trees divide, And screen from seeing and leave in sight
The ivy falls with the Bacchanal's hair
The wild vine slipping down leaves bare Her bright breast shortening into sighs; The wild vine slips with the weight of its leaves.
To the limbs that glitter, the feet that scare The wolf that follows, the fawn that flies.
What do ye singing? what is this ye sing?
Flowers bring we, and pure lips that please the gods,
Turn sharp with all its honey in our lips.
Night, a black hound, follows the white fawn day, Swifter than dreams the white flown feet of sleep;
And though the spring put back a little while Winter, and snows that plague all men for sin,
Spring shall be ruined with the rain, and storm Eat up like fire the ashen autumn days.
Who dream and die with dreaming; any god, Yea the least god of all things called divine,
Perchance by praying a man shall match his god. For if sleep have no mercy, and man's dreams
What shall this man do waking? By the gods, He shall not pray to dream sweet things to-night,
Queen, but what is it that hath burnt thine heart?
Look, ye say well, and know not what ye say,
And all my dreams to stuff that kindles it.
Yet one doth well being patient of the gods.
Yea, lest they smite us with some four-foot plague.
But when time spreads find out some herb for it.
And with their healing herbs infect our blood.
What ails thee to be jealous of their ways?
What if they give us poisonous drinks for wine?
They have their will; much talking mends it not.
And gall for milk, and cursing for a prayer?
Have they not given life, and the end of life?
Lo, where they heal, they help not; thus they do,
And we say prayers, and weep; but at the last, Sparing awhile, they smite and spare no whit.
Small praise man gets dispraising the high gods:
First Artemis for all this harried land

That mars with tooth and tusk and fiery feet Green pasturage and the grace of standing corn And meadow and marsh with springs and unblown leaves, Flocks and swift herds and all that bite sweet grass, I praise her not, what things are these to praise?
But when the king did sacrifice, and gave
Her not with bloodshed nor burnt-offering Revered he, nor with salt or cloven cake; Wherefore being wroth she plagued the land, but now
Which deed of these twain were not good to praise? For a just deed looks always either way
Yea, but a curse she hath sent above all these
Fire where the old fire went out, and where the wind Slackened, hath blown on us with deadlier air.
What storm is this that tightens all our sail?
Love, a thwart sea-wind full of rain and foam.
Whence blown, and born under what stormier star?
Southward across Euenus from the sea.
Thy speech turns toward Arcadia like blown wind.
Sharp as the north sets when the snows are out.
Nay, for this maiden hath no touch of love.
I would she had sought in some cold gulf of sea Love, or in dens where strange beasts lurk, or fire,
Where no spring is; I would she had sought therein And found, or ever love had found her here.
She is holier than all holy days or things,
Chaste, dedicated to pure prayers, and filled With higher thoughts than heaven; a maiden clean,
She loves not; what should one such do with love?
Look you, I speak not as one light of wit,
I hear my brothers wrangling in mid hall, And am not moved; and my son chiding them,
Foolish and wise men must be to the end, And feed myself with patience; but this most,
Love is one thing, an evil thing, and turns Choice words and wisdom into fire and air.
Sharp words and soul's division and fresh tears Flower-wise upon the old root of tears brought forth, Fruit-wise upon the old flower of tears sprung up,
These things are in my presage, and myself Am part of them and know not; but in dreams
Shed fire across my eyelids mixed with night, And burn me blind, and disilluminate
Darken with vision; seeing I see not, hear And hearing am not holpen, but mine eyes
Drawn up about my face that I may weep And the king wake not; and my brows and lips
That tremble, or water when it sobs with heat Kindled from under; and my tears fill my breast
With barren showers and salter than the sea, Such dreams divide me dreaming; for long since
Fire and a firebrand; this was ere my son, Meleager, a goodly flower in fields of fight,
Childlike; but yet he was not; and in time I bare him, and my heart was great; for yet
Nor queen so nobly bore as noble a thing As this my son was: such a birth God sent
Three weaving women, and span each a thread, Saying This for strength and That for luck, and one
So long shall this man see good days and live. And I with gathered raiment from the bed
Water, and trod the flame bare-foot, and crushed With naked hand spark beaten out of spark
These are the most high Fates that dwell with us, And we find favour a little in their sight,
Foils us; howbeit they have pitied me, O son, And thee most piteous, thee a tenderer thing
Wherefore I kissed and hid him with my hands, And covered under arms and hair, and wept, And feared to touch him with my tears, and laughed;
Men cast their heads back, seeing against the sun Blaze the armed man carven on his shield, and hear
Ring, as birds singing or flutes blown, and watch, High up, the cloven shadow of either plume
His helmet as a windy and wintering moon Seen through blown cloud and plume-like drift, when ships
Break, and the beaks dip under, drinking death; Yet was he then but a span long, and moaned
And with blind lips and fingers wrung my breast Hard, and thrust out with foolish hands and feet,
Who fright the gods frighted not him; he laughed Seeing them, and pushed out hands to feel and haul
Passed, and I hid the brand, and in my heart Laughed likewise, having all my will of heaven.
The gods have drawn us hither; for again I dreamt, and saw the black brand burst on fire
Fade flower-wise, and Death came and with dry lips Blew the charred ash into my breast; and Love
This I have also at heart; that not for me, Not for me only or son of mine, O girls,
Heart's love and heart's division; but for all There shines one sun and one wind blows till night.
And there is no light after, and no storm, But sleep and much forgetfulness of things.
Years hence, and heard high sayings of one most wise, Eurythemis my mother, who beheld
As one on earth disfleshed and disallied From breath or blood corruptible; such gifts
And equal face to all things, thus she said. But whatsoever intolerable or glad
Full of mine own soul, perfect of myself, Toward mine and me sufficient; and what chance
That shall we take, and that much bear withal. And now, before these gather to the hunt,
Lest love or some man's anger work him harm.
Before the beginning of years
Time, with a gift of tears, Grief, with a glass that ran;
Summer, with flowers that fell; Remembrance fallen from heaven,
Strength without hands to smite, Love that endures for a breath,
And life, the shadow of death.
Fire, and the falling of tears, And a measure of sliding sand
And froth and drift of the sea; And dust of the labouring earth;
In the houses of death and of birth; And wrought with weeping and laughter,
With life before and after And death beneath and above,
That his strength might endure for a span With travail and heavy sorrow,
From the winds of the north and the south
They breathed upon his mouth, They filled his body with life;
For the veils of the soul therein, A time for labour and thought,
They gave him light in his ways, And love, and a space for delight,
And night, and sleep in the night. His speech is a burning fire;
In his heart is a blind desire, In his eyes foreknowledge of death;
Sows, and he shall not reap, His life is a watch or a vision
O sweet new heaven and air without a star,
With deeds to do and praise to pluck from thee, Come forth a child, born with clear sound and light, With laughter and swift limbs and prosperous looks;
May leave thee memorable and us well sped.
Son, first I praise thy prayer, then bid thee speed;
And heed beyond all crying and sacrifice Light of things done and noise of labouring men.
Abide; for like rain-flakes in a wind they grow, The men thy fellows, and the choice of the world,
Thanks and safe days and peace in Calydon.
For the whole city and all the low-lying land Flames, and the soft air sounds with them that come;
Set thine eye thither and fix thy spirit and say Whom there thou knowest; for sharp mixed shadow and wind
With steam of steeds and flash of bridle or wheel, And fire, and parcels of the broken dawn,
That shine and shift as the edge of wild beasts' eyes, Smite upon mine; so fiery their blind edge
The first, for many I know not, being far off,
Sleeps the white sea-bred wife and silver-shod, Fair as fled foam, a goddess; and their son
Most like a god, full of the future fame.
Who are these shining like one sundered star?
Thy sister's sons, a double flower of men.
O sweetest kin to me in all the world,
Like kindled lights in untempestuous heaven, Fair flower-like stars on the iron foam of fight,
Even to the staining of both eyes with tears And kindling of warm eyelids with desire,
Seeing you so fair, and moulded like as gods. Far off ye come, and least in years of these,
Even such (for sailing hither I saw far hence,
Nigh Sparta with a strenuous-hearted stream) Even such I saw their sisters; one swan-white,
Fair Clytaemnestra, grave as pasturing fawns Who feed and fear some arrow; but at whiles,
She laughs and lightens with her eyes, and then Weeps; whereat Helen, having laughed, weeps too, And the other chides her, and she being chid speaks nought,
Laughing; so fare they, as in their bloomless bud And full of unblown life, the blood of gods.
Sweet days befall them and good loves and lords,
Peace, and a perfect life and blameless bed. But who shows next an eagle wrought in gold?
And with void mouth gapes after emptier prey?
Know by that sign the reign of Telamon Between the fierce mouths of the encountering brine
For like one great of hand he bears himself,
Glittering as wine and moving as a wave. But who girt round there roughly follows him?
Ancaeus, great of hand, an iron bulk,
Who drives against the surge of stormy spears Full-sailed; him Cepheus follows, his twin-born,
Praise be with men abroad; chaste lives with us,
Next by the left unsandalled foot know thou
Thy brethren, Toxeus and the violent-souled Plexippus, over-swift with hand and tongue;
Blows and corrupts their work with barren breath.
Speech too bears fruit, being worthy; and air blows down
And with charmed words and songs have men put out Wild evil, and the fire of tyrannies.
Yea, all things have they, save the gods and love.
Love thou the law and cleave to things ordained.
Law lives upon their lips whom these applaud.
How sayest thou these? what god applauds new things?
Zeus, who hath fear and custom under foot.
But loves not laws thrown down and lives awry.
Yet is not less himself than his own law.
Nor shifts and shuffles old things up and down.
But what he will remoulds and discreates.
Much, but not this, that each thing live its life.
Nor only live, but lighten and lift up higher.
Pride breaks itself, and too much gained is gone.
Things gained are gone, but great things done endure.
Child, if a man serve law through all his life
Praise; but who loves it only with his lips, And not in heart and deed desiring it
Him heaven infatuates and his twin-born fate Tracks, and gains on him, scenting sins far off,
Be man at one with equal-minded gods, So shall he prosper; not through laws torn up,
A woman armed makes war upon herself, Unwomanlike, and treads down use and wont
Love, and the cry of children, and the hand Trothplight and mutual mouth of marriages.
Not fire nor iron and the wide-mouthed wars Are deadlier than her lips or braided hair.
Falls from the other and burns the lives of men. But thou, son, be not filled with evil dreams,
Blind love burns out; but if one feed it full Till some discolouring stain dyes all his life,
The sweet wise death of old men honourable, Who have lived out all the length of all their years Blameless, and seen well-pleased the face of gods,
Things memorable, and while their days held out In sight of all men and the sun's great light
To the earth that bare them and the day that bred, Home friends and far-off hospitalities,
Lands loved of summer or washed by violent seas, Towns populous and many unfooted ways,
But when white age and venerable death Mow down the strength and life within their limbs,
Immortal honour is on them, having past Through splendid life and death desirable
Lands indiscoverable in the unheard-of west, Round which the strong stream of a sacred sea
There shows not her white wings and windy feet, Nor thunder nor swift rain saith anything, Nor the sun burns, but all things rest and thrive;
Sages and singers fiery from the god, And such as loved their land and all things good
Free lives and lips, free hands of men free-born, And whatsoever on earth was honourable
Live there a life no liker to the gods But nearer than their life of terrene days.
But from the light and fiery dreams of love Spring heavy sorrows and a sleepless life, Visions not dreams, whose lids no charm shall close
Crushes with sterile feet the unripening ear, Treads out the timeless vintage; whom do thou
Not without honour; and it shall bear to thee Such fruit as men reap from spent hours and wear,
Happiest, if thou submit thy soul to fate, And set thine eyes and heart on hopes high-born
So shalt thou be toward all men all thy days As light and might communicable, and burn
And break not as a man breaks nor burn down: For to whom other of all heroic names
And gloriously hast thou lived, and made thy life To me that bare thee and to all men born
When wild wars broke all round thy father's house, And the mad people of windy mountain ways
Aetolia thundered with Thessalian hoofs; Yet these, as wind baffles the foam, and beats Straight back the relaxed ripple, didst thou break
And man from man they fell; for ye twain stood God against god, Ares and Artemis,
A sharp-toothed curse thou too shalt overcome; For in the greener blossom of thy life Ere the full blade caught flower, and when time gave
But with great hand and heart seek praise of men Out of sharp straits and many a grievous thing,
On channels never sailed in, and by shores Where the old winds cease not blowing, and all the night
Meleager, a noble wisdom and fair words
O mother, I am not fain to strive in speech
Even as they say and full of sacred words. But one thing I know surely, and cleave to this;
Nor womanlike to weave sweet words, and melt Mutable minds of wise men as with fire,
Shall not want wit to see what things be right. For whom they love and whom reject, being gods,
Submits himself, refraining all his heart. And I too as thou sayest have seen great things;
First caught between stretched ropes the roaring west, And all our oars smote eastward, and the wind
White splendid snow-flakes of the sundering foam, And the first furrow in virginal green sea
And closed, as when deep sleep subdues man's breath Lips close and heart subsides; and closing, shone
Round many a trembling mouth of doubtful gods, Risen out of sunless and sonorous gulfs
That watched us; and when flying the dove was snared As with men's hands, but we shot after and sped
And chiefliest when hoar beach and herbless cliff Stood out ahead from Colchis, and we heard Clefts hoarse with wind, and saw through narrowing reefs
Flash, and the white wet flame of breakers burn Far under a kindling south-wind, as a lamp

Wild heights untravelled of the wind, and vales Cloven seaward by their violent streams, and white With bitter flowers and bright salt scurf of brine; Heard sweep their sharp swift gales, and bowing bird-wise
Tread loose the long skirts of a storm; and saw The whole white Euxine clash together and fall Full-mouthed, and thunderous from a thousand throats;
Medea, deadlier than the sea; but there Seeing many a wonder and fearful things to men
Most fair and fearful, feminine, a god, Faultless; whom I that love not, being unlike, Fear, and give honour, and choose from all the gods.
Lady, the daughter of Thestius, and thou, son,
Scared with vain dreams and fluttering like spent fire, I come to judge between you, but a king

For what lies light on many and they forget, Small things and transitory as a wind o' the sea,
A man in arms, strong and a joy to men Seeing thine head glitter and thine hand burn its way Through a heavy and iron furrow of sundering spears;
The small one thing that lying drew down my life To lie with thee and feed thee; a child and weak,
Who then sought to thee? who gat help? who knew If thou wert goodly? nay, no man at all.
Child? or what strange land shone with war through thee? But fair for me thou wert, O little life, Fruitless, the fruit of mine own flesh, and blind,

I charge thee by thy soul and this my breast, Fear thou the gods and me and thine own heart,
What wind upon what wave of altering time Shall speak a storm and blow calamity?
But the gods break it; yet not less, fair son, If but one thing be stronger, if one endure,
That burns between us, going from me to thee, Shall more endure than all things. What dost thou, Following strange loves? why wilt thou kill mine heart?
From my clear wits, and seem of mine own self Dethroned, dispraised, disseated; and my mind, That was my crown, breaks, and mine heart is gone,
Ashamed, as a mean woman; take thou thought: Live if thou wilt, and if thou wilt not, look,
Thou shalt not die as men die, but thine end Fallen upon thee shall break me unaware.
Queen, my whole heart is molten with thy tears,

For the gods very subtly fashion Madness with sadness upon earth:
Nor holding pity of any worth; And many things they have given and taken,
The firm land have they loosed and shaken, And sealed the sea with all her springs;

Put moans into the bridal measure And on the bridal wools a stain,

What shall be done with all these tears of ours?
To bathe the brows of morning? or like flowers Be shed and shine before the starriest hours,
Or rather, O our masters, shall they be Food for the famine of the grievous sea,
Satiating the sad gods? or fall and flow Among the years and seasons to and fro,
And fill them full with grieving ere they go? Alas, our lords, and yet alas again,
But all we smite thereat in vain, Smite the gates barred with groanings manifold,
Yea, and with weariness of lips and eyes, With breaking of the bosom, and with sighs,
And filled with days we would not fain behold And nights we would not hear of, we wax old,
We are outcast, strayed between bright sun and moon; Our light and darkness are as leaves of flowers, Black flowers and white, that perish; and the noon--
A little fruit a little while is ours, And the worm finds it soon.
Lay hands upon the draught that quickeneth, Fulfilled with all tears shed and all things done,
The bubbling bitterness of life and death, And hold it to our lips and laugh; but they
Lest they too change and sleep, the fates that spun, The lips that made us and the hands that slay; Lest all these change, and heaven bow down to none,
And terrene revolution of the sun. Therefore they thrust it from them, putting time away.
With multitudinous days and nights and tears And many mixing savours of strange years,
Cast out and spilt about their holy places: That life were given them as a fruit to eat
Might ebb, drawn backward from their eyes, and night Hide for one hour the imperishable faces.
Sorrow and sleep, one paler than young snow, One cold as blight of dew and ruinous rain,
Awhile as all things born with us and we, And grieve as men, and like slain men be slain.
The gods are gracious, praising God; and one, When hast thou seen? or hast thou felt his breath
Nor fill thee to the lips with fiery death? None hath beheld him, none
Swift without feet and flying without wings, Intolerable, not clad with death or life,
The lord of love and loathing and of strife Who gives a star and takes a sun away;
To the earthly body and grievous growth of clay; Who turns the large limbs to a little flame
Who makes desire, and slays desire with shame; Who shakes the heaven as ashes in his hand;
Bids day waste night as fire devours a brand, Smites without sword, and scourges without rod;
Yea, with thine hate, O God, thou hast covered us,
And made us transitory and hazardous, Light things and slight; Yet have men praised thee, saying, He hath made man thus,
Thou hast kissed us, and hast smitten; thou hast laid Upon us with thy left hand life, and said, Live: and again thou hast said, Yield up your breath,

Thou hast sent us sleep, and stricken sleep with dreams, Saying, Joy is not, but love of joy shall be, Thou hast made sweet springs for all the pleasant streams, In the end thou hast made them bitter with the sea.

Thou hast marred one face with fire of many tears; Thou hast taken love, and given us sorrow again; With pain thou hast filled us full to the eyes and ears. Therefore because thou art strong, our father, and we
Constrains us in the shallows of the sea And breaks us at the limits of the land;
And loosed the hours like arrows; and let fall Sins and wild words and many a winged woe
Because thou hast made the thunder, and thy feet Are as a rushing water when the skies
And flames of fire the eyelids of thine eyes; Because thou art over all who are over us;
Because thou art cruel and men are piteous, And our hands labour and thine hand scattereth;
Lo, with ephemeral lips and casual breath, At least we witness of thee ere we die
That each man in his heart sigheth, and saith, That all men even as I, All we are against thee, against thee, O God most high,
Your lips from over-speech, Loud words and longing are so little worth;
For silence after grievous things is good, And reverence, and the fear that makes men whole,
And lordship of the soul. But from sharp words and wits men pluck no fruit,
For words divide and rend; But silence is most noble till the end.

Praised be all gods that look toward Calydon.

A maiden's and a prophet's and thy son's.

Slept no soft sleep, with violent visions fed, The blind bulk of the immeasurable beast. And seeing, he shuddered with sharp lust of praise Through all his limbs, and launched a double dart,
Too hot of spirit and feebler than his will, That his hand failed, though fervent; and the shaft,
Shook, and stuck fast; then all abode save one, The Arcadian Atalanta; from her side Sprang her hounds, labouring at the leash, and slipped,

His tense flank trembling round the barbed wound, Hateful, and fiery with invasive eyes

Sweet words long since and loved me will not speak Nor love nor look upon me; and all my life
